transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I guess... I'm just here because I keep messing up little things. Just... small mistakes. Like, at the senior center, I'll write down the wrong time on the class sign-up sheet. Or... I'll be doing some woodworking, measure a board, and still cut it a bit short. Just... skipping over the small print, I suppose. That's about it.
When you make these mistakes with small details or small print, is it that you're having trouble seeing clearly, or is it more that you're overlooking things even though you can see them fine?

No, my eyes are fine. I mean, I wear my reading glasses, so I can see it clearly enough. I just... I guess I just overlook things. Like I was saying with the measuring tape or the sign-up sheets... I just miss it.
Besides these mistakes with small details, have you noticed any problems with your memory — like forgetting things you normally would remember, or having trouble concentrating on tasks?
No, not really. Memory seems okay, I think. I mean, I don't forget where I put my keys or anything like that. Just... the other stuff I mentioned.

When you make these mistakes — like cutting the board short or missing things on the sign-up sheet — do you tend to miss things on one particular side, like always on the left or always on the right? Or does it happen randomly all over?
I don't think so. It's just... random, I guess. Not one side or the other. Just wherever.

When you're looking at something — like reading a page or looking at an object in front of you — do you ever notice that part of it seems to be missing or cut off, like you can't see one edge or corner even when you're looking straight at it?
No, I... I haven't noticed anything like that. I can see the whole page fine. Nothing's cut off.

When you're sitting at a table or in a room, do you ever notice that you miss things on one side of your body — like not seeing someone sitting to your left, or bumping into furniture on one side — even though nothing is wrong with your eyes?
No... I don't think so. I haven't really had any problems like that. Just... seeing things fine. I don't bump into things.

When you're reading or doing detailed work, does it feel like you're having trouble paying attention or concentrating on the task itself, or does it feel more like your eyes are just not picking up the details even though you're trying to look carefully?
I think... it's just the concentrating part. My eyes are fine, I just... my mind wanders off, I guess. I just lose focus.
Have you always had this trouble with concentration and focus, or is this something that's gotten worse recently?

I guess it's always been like this. Um... even back in elementary school, my teachers used to write things on my report cards. They'd say I was bright, but... I'd always forget my books, or lose my homework. Just... staring out the window, mostly. Unless someone was right there to keep me on track, I'd just drift. So... no, it's not a recent thing.

Besides the mistakes you mentioned, do you find yourself interrupting people when they're talking, or acting without thinking things through first? And does this kind of thing cause problems for you in your daily life now?

No... I don't really interrupt people. I keep to myself, mostly. 

But as for problems... I guess the mix-ups get in the way sometimes. I actually had to step back from helping lead a couple of DIY workshops recently. And... well, my wife usually has to double-check our plans now. Just to make sure I don't throw off family visits or things we do at the center. So... yeah, I suppose it causes some issues.
Do you find yourself fidgeting a lot, having trouble sitting still, or feeling like you have excess energy that's hard to control?

Not really excess energy, no. But... I guess I don't sit still all that well. If I have to sit through a whole meeting, or... even just a quiet evening at the condo, I get this... ants-in-my-pants feeling. I usually just want to get up and putter around. Check on things. But... that's about it.

You mentioned stepping back from the workshops and your wife double-checking plans — going back further, did you have similar kinds of problems in school or at work when you were younger? Like, did teachers or bosses ever mention that your carelessness or lack of focus was affecting your grades or job performance?

I don't know... I guess so. I mean, my grades were never great. Teachers always said I wasn't applying myself. And... well, I've had a few jobs over the years where things didn't work out. Mostly just... small mistakes adding up, I suppose. But I got by.
You mentioned getting an 'ants-in-your-pants' feeling and needing to get up and putter around. How often does that happen — is it something you deal with most days, or just occasionally?
I don't really know... I don't keep track of it. Just... occasionally, I guess. It's not really something I pay much attention to.

You mentioned losing focus at work, in school, and at home. Are these concentration problems something you notice pretty much everywhere you go — like at the senior center, during family visits, when you're with friends — or are there certain places or situations where you can focus better?
I'm not really sure. I don't think about it much when I'm out... or visiting people. It's just kind of how things are, I guess. I haven't really noticed if one place is better than another.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a lifelong pattern of inattention, carelessness with details, and difficulty sustaining focus that began in elementary school and persists into older adulthood. Core symptoms include overlooking details despite adequate vision and cognition, losing focus during tasks, mind wandering, forgetfulness of materials, and difficulty maintaining attention without external structure. While hyperactivity symptoms are minimal and non-impairing (occasional restlessness without excess energy), the prominent and pervasive inattention symptoms across multiple life domains (school, work, family, hobbies) with documented functional impairment (stepped back from workshops, wife must verify plans) meets criteria for ADHD, Predominantly Inattentive Type. The lifelong course and cross-situational presentation support this diagnosis over acquired attention difficulties.
